report:
# AI-Accelerated Materials Workflows on the M-AI-Synth Prototype Dataset: Graph-Network Property Prediction, VAE Structure Generation and Bayesian Optimisation of Synthesis Conditions

*Autonomous research report. All code is in `code/`, intermediate results in `outputs/`, figures in `report/images/`.*

---

## Abstract

The M-AI-Synth file is a small prototyping dataset with one block per canonical AI-for-materials workflow: (i) **property prediction** from an atomic graph, (ii) **generation** of lattice parameters, and (iii) **autonomous optimisation** of a synthesis temperature/time recipe. I implemented all three end-to-end in pure NumPy/SciPy, since no deep-learning framework was available. The models are a crystal-graph convolutional network (CGCNN-style) with hand-written back-propagation, a variational auto-encoder (VAE), and a Gaussian-process Bayesian optimiser (GP-BO). Analytic gradients agree with finite differences to a relative error of ≤5×10⁻⁶. Main results:

1. **Property prediction.** On a structure-dependent benchmark of 5 000 simulated 5-atom clusters built on the dataset's K5 graph template, the trained GNN predicts a surrogate formation energy with a test **MAE of 8.1 meV/atom (R² = 0.999)**. The comparisons are 303 meV/atom for the mean predictor and 37.8 meV/atom for the best hand-crafted ridge model. Removing or shuffling the interatomic-distance edge features raises the error to 277 / 280 meV/atom, so the network relies on geometry. On the 97 *provided* targets the same network does not beat the mean predictor (MAE 0.546 vs 0.541 eV/atom). The cause is a data artefact: the targets repeat exactly with period 8 and carry no learnable structure–property relation, and an index-mod-8 lookup reaches 0.10 eV/atom.
2. **Structure generation.** A β-VAE trained on the 101 (a, b) lattice pairs generates new lattices with mean 5.52–5.54 Å and spread 0.21–0.25 Å (data: 5.52 ± 0.27 Å). It reaches 100 % coverage, 88–93 % precision and 100 % physical validity, and 71–96 % of samples are novel (>0.02 Å from every training pair). It recovers 38–52 % of held-out lattices in leave-2-of-7-out tests, while a memoriser recovers 0 %.
3. **Autonomous optimisation.** With the dataset's noise level (σ = 0.1, i.e. 10 yield-percentage points), GP-UCB recommends a recipe within a median **|ΔT| = 4.9 °C and |Δt| = 0.39 min** of the true optimum (350 °C, 20 min) after 25 experiments, at a median true yield of **99.0 %**. The median true yield is 87–89 % for random and Latin-hypercube search (Wilcoxon p < 10⁻⁴). The gain over the baselines persists when the optimum is placed at random (GP-UCB 98.0 % vs ≤89.5 %).

---

## 1. Introduction and related work

Data-driven materials discovery combines three capabilities.

- **Forward models** predict properties from structure. The Materials Project (Jain *et al.*, 2013; `related_work/paper_000.pdf`) supplies the DFT databases, and crystal-graph convolutional neural networks (CGCNN; Xie & Grossman, 2018; `paper_002.pdf`) learn formation energies directly from the atomic connectivity and interatomic distances of a crystal graph.
- **Generative/inverse models** propose new structures.
- **Closed-loop optimisation** of synthesis/processing parameters cuts down trial-and-error experimentation. Raccuglia *et al.* (2016; `paper_003.pdf`) showed that models trained on failed as well as successful syntheses can guide exploratory reactions. Physics-informed ML (Karniadakis *et al.*, 2021; `paper_001.pdf`) argues for embedding physical structure (symmetries, energy functions, units) into such models when data are scarce.

The provided dataset is a minimal stand-in for this multimodal setting. Its three blocks are named after three demo scripts (`property_prediction.py`, `structure_generation.py`, `autonomous_optimization.py`). The goal was to reproduce each workflow with a properly trained model, report its headline metric in physical units, and validate it against baselines and leakage/memorisation controls.

---

## 2. Data overview and audit

`code/01_audit.py` parses the file (three `#` headers, one Python list per line; the parser asserts 4/2/6 lines per block) and writes `outputs/data_audit.json`.

| Block | Array | Length | Content (verified) |
|---|---|---|---|
| property prediction | atomic numbers | 100 | all Z = 5 (boron) |
| | node features | 117 | exact 13 × 9 grid, x = −2 + 0.2·r + 0.5·c (max error 4×10⁻¹⁶); 61 unique values |
| | edge list | 20 ints = 10 edges | complete graph **K5** on 5 nodes |
| | targets | 97 | 22 unique values; **exactly periodic with period 8 from index 15**; mean 0.084, sd 0.579 |
| structure generation | lattice a | 101 | 7 unique values (5.1234–5.9012), period 7 |
| | lattice b | 101 | = lattice a shifted by 4 → only **7 unique (a,b) pairs** |
| optimisation | T range, t range | 2, 2 | T ∈ [200, 500] °C, t ∈ [10, 30] min |
| | optimum, noise, n_iter | 1 each | (350 °C, 20 min), σ = 0.1, 10 iterations |

![Data overview](images/fig1_data_overview.png)

**Figure 1.** (a) The 97 property targets; the shaded region marks the exact period-8 regime. (b) The node-feature vector reshaped to its 13 × 9 linear grid. (c) The edge list is the complete graph K5 over five boron atoms. (d, e) The two lattice arrays are cyclic shifts of one 7-value sequence, giving 7 distinct (a,b) pairs. (f) Target histogram.

**Implications.** The three arrays of the property block have no defined mapping between them (100 / 117 / 97 entries). They also contain no coordinates or chemical variety, and the target is a function of its list position. The provided block therefore cannot show that a GNN learns a structure–property relation. I handled this with two tracks:

- **Track A** trains the GNN on the provided data under an explicit alignment assumption and reports the result honestly.
- **Track B** builds a structure-dependent benchmark from the same K5 template, where learning is meaningful.

Assumed units are eV/atom for the targets, Å for the lattice parameters, and yield fraction for the optimisation response.

---

## 3. Methods

### 3.1 Property prediction: CGCNN-style message-passing network (`code/gnn_np.py`)

Each material is a graph of N = 5 atoms with the dataset's K5 adjacency A. Node inputs x_i are an element one-hot (Track B) or [one-hot(Z=5), descriptor] (Track A). Edge inputs e_ij are a Gaussian radial-basis expansion of the interatomic distance: 21 centres from 0.5 to 4.5 Å, width 0.2 Å, as in CGCNN. One convolution layer is (Xie & Grossman 2018, Eq. 5, without batch-norm)

  z_ij = h_i W_a + h_j W_b + e_ij W_e + b,  m_ij = σ(z_ij^f) ⊙ softplus(z_ij^s),  h_i ← softplus(h_i + Σ_j A_ij m_ij).

The network is: an embedding layer (24 channels), 3 conv layers, mean pooling to a cluster embedding, then softplus-MLP(32) → scalar. Forward and backward passes are written by hand in NumPy. A finite-difference check gives a maximum relative gradient error of 9.6×10⁻⁸ on random inputs and 5.1×10⁻⁶ on the real RBF features. Training minimises the MSE on standardised targets with Adam (lr 3×10⁻³, cosine decay, batch 128). The model with the best validation loss is kept. The seed is fixed (0).

**Track B: simulated structure-dependent set** (`code/02_gnn_trackB.py`)

- *Clusters.* 5 000 five-atom clusters on the K5 template. Elements are drawn from {Li, B, C, N, O} (Z = 3, 5, 6, 7, 8). Geometries are trigonal bipyramids scaled to the mean covalent bond length × U(0.85, 1.25), with N(0, 0.18 Å) Gaussian jitter of every coordinate.
- *Surrogate formation energy per atom* (documented, physically motivated):
  E_f = (1/N)[ Σ_{i<j} D_ij((1−e^{−α(r_ij−r⁰_ij)})² − 1) − k Σ_{i<j}(χ_i−χ_j)²/r_ij + Σ_i Δμ_{Z_i} ] + ε,
  - D_ij = √(D_i D_j) and r⁰_ij = R_i + R_j (covalent radii);
  - α = 1.6 Å⁻¹;
  - Pauling electronegativities χ give an ionic stabilisation term with k = 0.35 eV·Å;
  - element reference offsets Δμ;
  - label noise ε ~ N(0, 5 meV/atom).
- *Resulting data.* E_f spans −2.15 to 0.19 eV/atom (sd 0.363 eV/atom).
- *Training.* Split 4000/500/500; 150 epochs.
- *Baselines.* Mean predictor; ridge on composition (element counts); ridge on composition + sorted pair distances + inverse distances + element-pair counts (a strong hand-crafted descriptor model).
- *Ablations.* The same GNN (100 epochs) with distance features removed (topology + composition only) or randomly shuffled across clusters.
- *Learning curve.* n_train ∈ {250, 500, 1000, 2000} (100 epochs) and 4000 (150 epochs).

**Track A: provided data** (`code/03_gnn_trackA.py`)

- *Alignment assumption.* Sample i is the K5 boron graph whose 5 node descriptors are `node_features[i:i+5]` (a sliding window that uses indices 0–100 for i = 0–96). There are no coordinates, so there are no edge features.
- *Model and evaluation.* GNN with 16 channels and 2 layers, trained for 300 epochs, evaluated on 10 random 77/10/10 splits and on one blocked split (last 20 % of indices as test).
- *Controls.* Mean predictor; linear model on the 5 descriptors; the GNN refit with scrambled training labels; an index-mod-8 lookup table that tests for leakage through list position.

### 3.2 Structure generation: variational auto-encoder (`code/04_vae.py`)

- *Inputs.* The (a, b) pairs, standardised with the training mean/sd (5.520/5.521 Å, 0.273/0.270 Å).
- *Architecture.* Encoder 2→16→16→(μ, log σ²) ∈ ℝ²×ℝ² and decoder 2→16→16→2, both with tanh activations.
- *Training.* Loss = squared reconstruction error + β·KL(q(z|x) ‖ N(0, I)), with a linear KL warm-up over the first 30 % of 3 000 full-batch Adam epochs (lr 3×10⁻³). β ∈ {0.1, 1}. Reparameterised gradients are hand-coded and checked (relative error 9.4×10⁻⁷).
- *Generation.* Draw z ~ N(0, I), decode, and **invert the standardisation back to Å**.
- *Metrics* (3 000 samples):
  - marginal Wasserstein-1 distances;
  - RBF-MMD (bandwidth 0.1 Å);
  - a smoothed 2-D histogram KL(data ‖ generated);
  - kNN precision/coverage (Naeem *et al.* 2020, k = 1, on the 7 unique pairs);
  - novelty (fraction > 0.02 Å from every training pair);
  - validity (both parameters within 5.0–6.0 Å).
- *Comparison generators.* A **memoriser** (resampling training rows), a Gaussian and a KDE (bandwidth 0.08 Å).
- *Generalisation test.* **Leave-2-of-7-out rediscovery**: for all 21 pairs of held-out lattices, retrain on the remaining five and measure the distance from the closest of 3 000 generated samples to each held-out lattice.

### 3.3 Autonomous optimisation: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimisation (`code/05_bo.py`)

The file gives the bounds, optimum, noise and iteration count but not the response surface. I assumed a Gaussian yield peak:

  yield(T, t) = exp(−½[((T−T*)/50 °C)² + ((t−t*)/5 min)²]),  observation = yield + N(0, 0.1²),

with (T*, t*) = (350 °C, 20 min). Because yield is a fraction, the noise of 0.1 means 10 percentage points.

- *GP model.* ARD-RBF kernel on unit-scaled inputs with standardised outputs. Hyper-parameters come from maximising the marginal likelihood (L-BFGS-B, 3 restarts), with a length-scale floor of 0.1 so the model cannot chase single noisy points.
- *Acquisition.* Expected Improvement (EI) or UCB (μ + 2σ), maximised over 3 000 random candidates.
- *Recommendation.* The evaluated recipe with the highest posterior mean. Baselines (random, Latin hypercube, randomly ordered 5 × 5 grid) recommend their best *observed* recipe.
- *Budget.* 5 LHS initial points + 20 sequential experiments, with the dataset's n_iter = 10 marked.
- *Seeds and scenarios.* 20 seeds × 3 scenarios: nominal; randomised optimum in the inner 80 % of the box with σ = 0.1; randomised optimum with σ = 0.02. The randomised scenarios remove the advantage a centred grid gets from a centred optimum.
- *Evaluation.* All methods are scored on the **true (noise-free) yield of the recommended recipe**, in %. Comparisons use paired one-sided Wilcoxon tests across seeds.

---

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Property prediction with a trained graph network

**Track B: structure-dependent benchmark (canonical result).** The trained CGCNN predicts the surrogate formation energy of 500 held-out clusters with **MAE = 8.1 meV/atom, RMSE = 12.5 meV/atom and R² = 0.9988**. The prediction range is −2.15 to 0.19 eV/atom, and the irreducible label-noise floor is an MAE of 4.0 meV/atom.

![GNN Track B](images/fig2_gnn_trackB.png)

**Figure 2.** CGCNN on 5 000 simulated K5 clusters.
- (a) Training and validation MSE per epoch, in physical units (eV²/atom²), for the full model and the two ablations. Validation follows training down by three orders of magnitude. The best validation epoch is 142 of 150, and the train/val gap stays small, so the model does not over-fit.
- (b) Parity of predicted vs. surrogate E_f on the test set for the GNN and for the best descriptor-ridge model.
- (c) Test MAE vs. training-set size, with the baselines drawn as dashed lines.

| Model (test set, n = 500) | MAE (meV/atom) | RMSE (meV/atom) | R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean predictor | 303.0 | 367.6 | −0.005 |
| Ridge, composition only | 291.7 | 352.2 | 0.077 |
| Ridge, composition + sorted distances + 1/r + pair counts | 37.8 | 53.5 | 0.979 |
| GNN, distance features removed (composition + K5 topology) | 276.9 | 328.5 | 0.197 |
| GNN, distance features shuffled across clusters | 280.1 | 332.4 | 0.178 |
| **GNN (full CGCNN, 4 000 training clusters)** | **8.1** | **12.5** | **0.9988** |

*Structure dependence.*
- The GNN error is 37 times lower than the mean predictor's and 4.7 times lower than the strongest hand-engineered linear model's.
- Composition alone explains less than 20 % of the variance (composition ridge R² = 0.08; distance-free GNN R² = 0.20).
- When distances are shuffled across clusters, the GNN falls to the composition-only level. It therefore uses the actual interatomic geometry of each cluster, not merely the presence of distance features.

*Data efficiency.* The learning curve (Fig. 2c) decreases monotonically: 92, 36, 24 and 20 meV/atom for 250, 500, 1 000 and 2 000 training clusters at 100 epochs, and 8.1 meV/atom for 4 000 clusters at 150 epochs. With 500 training clusters the GNN already matches the descriptor-ridge model trained on 4 000.

![GNN embeddings and ablations](images/fig3_gnn_ablation_embedding.png)

**Figure 3.** (a) First two principal components of the learned 24-dimensional cluster embeddings (after pooling) for the test set, coloured by E_f. The embedding orders clusters smoothly by energy, and its mean per-channel sd across graphs is 1.79, so the embedding has not collapsed. (b) Test MAE of the ablations and baselines.

**Track A: provided property block (honest result).**

![GNN on provided data](images/fig4_gnn_trackA_provided.png)

**Figure 4.** The same network trained on the 97 provided targets.
- (a) Loss curves for one split: the training loss decreases but the validation MSE never drops clearly below the target variance.
- (b) Test MAE over 10 random splits.
- (c) Blocked split: the GNN predicts nearly the mean, while the index-mod-8 lookup follows the oscillation exactly.

| Model (provided data) | random splits, MAE (eV/atom), mean ± sd | blocked split MAE (eV/atom) |
|---|---|---|
| Mean predictor | 0.541 ± 0.074 | 0.506 |
| Linear on 5 window descriptors | 0.578 ± 0.079 | n/a |
| GNN (K5, Z = 5, descriptor nodes) | 0.546 ± 0.072 | 0.501 |
| GNN trained on scrambled labels | 0.565 ± 0.105 | n/a |
| *Index mod 8 lookup (leakage control, not a model)* | *0.102 ± 0.058* | *0.054* |

*Comparison with the mean.* The GNN trains correctly: its embeddings vary across graphs (sd 0.5–1.0), and the training loss decreases. It still does not outperform the mean predictor (it wins in 6 of 10 splits, by 0.005 eV/atom on average), and it is no better than its scrambled-label control.

*Why.* All atoms are boron, there are no coordinates, and the descriptor window varies only linearly with the list index. Meanwhile the target repeats exactly every 8 entries, and an index-mod-8 lookup alone reaches 0.10 eV/atom. The provided targets therefore contain no learnable structure–property signal; they are a placeholder sequence. Track B is the meaningful demonstration of the property-prediction workflow.

### 4.2 Structure generation with a VAE

![VAE](images/fig5_vae.png)

**Figure 5.** VAE on lattice parameters.
- (a) Reconstruction (solid) and KL (dashed) losses per epoch for β = 0.1 and 1. The grey curve is the KL warm-up schedule. During warm-up the reconstruction error rises as the KL term compresses the posterior: this is the expected rate–distortion trade-off, not divergence.
- (b) Latent means of the training pairs, coloured by a, with 1σ posterior ellipses. The 7 lattices occupy distinct, ordered regions of latent space.
- (c) The decoded a over the latent plane is smooth.
- (d–f) Generated vs. training marginals and the joint (a, b) distribution, in Å.

| Generator | mean a / b (Å) | sd a / b (Å) | W1 a / b (Å) | MMD | precision | coverage | novelty | valid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **VAE β = 0.1** | 5.537 / 5.520 | 0.254 / 0.247 | 0.034 / 0.034 | 0.011 | 0.93 | 1.00 | 0.71 | 1.00 |
| **VAE β = 1** | 5.517 / 5.516 | 0.209 / 0.221 | 0.071 / 0.063 | 0.075 | 0.88 | 1.00 | 0.96 | 1.00 |
| Memoriser | 5.521 / 5.517 | 0.271 / 0.270 | 0.002 / 0.004 | 0.000 | 1.00 | 1.00 | **0.00** | 1.00 |
| Gaussian | 5.517 / 5.529 | 0.271 / 0.270 | 0.070 / 0.069 | 0.137 | 0.42 | 1.00 | 0.99 | 0.88 |
| KDE (0.08 Å) | 5.524 / 5.521 | 0.284 / 0.282 | 0.037 / 0.037 | 0.027 | 0.93 | 1.00 | 0.96 | 0.95 |
| *training data* | *5.520 / 5.521* | *0.273 / 0.270* | | | | | | |

*Generated lattices.* Generated lattices are in physical units: means of 5.52–5.54 Å, sd 0.21–0.25 Å, every sample inside the physically plausible 5.0–6.0 Å window, and all 7 training lattices covered. They are not copies. With β = 0.1 the VAE matches the data distribution closely (W1 ≈ 0.034 Å per axis, MMD 0.011, below KDE) while still placing 71 % of samples more than 0.02 Å from any training pair; reconstruction MAE is 0.010 Å. With β = 1 the latent space is smoother and novelty rises to 96 %, at the cost of a wider spread between the discrete training lattices (W1 ≈ 0.07 Å, MMD 0.075).

*Interpolation along a manifold.* Figure 5f shows that the VAE does not scatter isotropically like the Gaussian baseline (precision 0.42, 12 % invalid). It generates new lattices along a continuous one-dimensional manifold that threads through the training lattices, which amounts to a learned, Vegard-like interpolation between known structures.

![VAE validation](images/fig6_vae_validation.png)

**Figure 6.** (a) Precision, coverage, novelty and validity of the generators. (b) Leave-2-of-7-out rediscovery: the fraction of held-out lattices that a generator trained without them produces within 0.05 Å (dark) or 0.10 Å (light), over 21 folds.

*Rediscovery.* The memoriser has perfect fidelity scores (W1 ≈ 0.003 Å, MMD ≈ 0, precision 1) yet zero novelty and zero rediscovery. Fidelity metrics alone reward copying, so novelty and held-out tests are needed. The VAE rediscovers 38 % (β = 0.1) and 33 % (β = 1) of held-out lattices within 0.05 Å, and 52 % / 48 % within 0.10 Å; the median closest distance is 0.09–0.12 Å.

*KDE comparison.* The KDE scores higher on this test (83 % within 0.05 Å), and this has to be read carefully. The held-out lattices sit about 0.16 Å from their nearest retained neighbours. An isotropic KDE with a 0.08 Å bandwidth puts some of its 3 000 samples there by chance, through spread rather than through structural inference; it also produces 5 % invalid lattices, while the VAE produces none. With only 7 distinct training structures, no generator can be expected to infer genuinely new chemistry. What the VAE learns is a smooth, valid interpolation manifold.

### 4.3 Autonomous optimisation of synthesis temperature and time

\*The 5 × 5 grid contains (350 °C, 20 min) exactly, because the nominal optimum lies at the centre of the box. Its perfect nominal score is a benchmark artefact, and it disappears once the optimum is randomised.

*Nominal scenario.* At the dataset's noise level, both GP-BO variants find a recipe at ≥ 98.5 % median true yield after 25 experiments, against 87–89 % for random and LHS search (paired Wilcoxon: GP-EI > Random p = 7×10⁻⁵, GP-EI > LHS p = 1×10⁻⁵, GP-UCB > Random/LHS p = 2×10⁻⁵). *Seed-0 run.* In the GP-EI run shown in Fig. 8, the recommended recipe after 25 experiments is **T = 344.8 °C, t = 19.3 min**: 5.2 °C and 0.7 min from the true optimum, at a true yield of 98.4 %. The fitted unit-scale length-scales (0.23, 0.34) correspond to 68 °C and 6.7 min, close to the true peak widths of 50 °C and 5 min.

*Randomised optimum.* GP-UCB still beats every baseline (p ≤ 0.004). GP-EI beats random and grid search (p = 0.05 and 0.02) but its margin over LHS is not significant at σ = 0.1 (p = 0.24): EI sometimes commits early to a noisy local maximum. At σ = 0.02, both GP methods recover the optimum to within about 2 °C and 0.15 min in 95 % of runs.

![BO offsets](images/fig9_bo_offsets.png)

**Figure 9.** The final recommended recipe relative to the true optimum (ΔT, Δt) for every seed and method. The dashed ellipse is the 95 %-yield contour.

---

## 5. Validation and controls

1. **Gradient correctness.** All three learned models (GNN, VAE, and the GP's likelihood optimised with L-BFGS-B) train on analytic gradients. Hand-coded back-propagation agrees with central finite differences to ≤5×10⁻⁶ relative error (GNN 5.1×10⁻⁶, VAE 9.4×10⁻⁷).
2. **The GNN uses structure.**
   - In Track B the embedding standard deviation across test clusters is 1.79 (> 0), so the network does not collapse to the mean.
   - Validation loss tracks training loss (Fig. 2a) with no sign of over-fitting.
   - Shuffling distances across clusters removes most of the skill.
3. **Leakage in the provided targets.** The index-mod-8 lookup reaches 0.10 eV/atom MAE (random splits) and 0.054 eV/atom (blocked split), while every structure/descriptor-based model scores ≈ 0.50–0.58 eV/atom. The y-scrambled GNN scores the same as the real one. The provided targets therefore encode list position, not structure (Fig. 4).
4. **Memorisation in generation.** The memoriser baseline and the leave-out tests show that the VAE's fidelity is not obtained by copying (§4.2).
5. **Benchmark artefact in optimisation.** Randomising the optimum location shows that the grid's perfect nominal score is an artefact, while the BO advantage persists (§4.3).

---

## 6. Discussion

*What the three workflows show.*

- *GNN.* A CGCNN-type network trained end-to-end learns a formation-energy function of composition **and** geometry from graph data. Its errors (8.1 meV/atom) fall far below the composition-only limit and well below a strong descriptor-ridge model. This is the mechanism that lets CGCNN reach DFT-level accuracy on Materials Project data.
- *VAE.* The VAE turns 7 discrete lattices into a continuous, valid latent manifold that can be sampled and inverted to physical units. It is a minimal version of latent-space inverse design.
- *GP-BO.* GP-BO reaches a near-optimal synthesis recipe (≥ 98 % yield, within about 5 °C / 0.5 min) in 25 noisy experiments. Space-filling designs stay at about 88 %. This is the experimental-cost saving that motivates autonomous laboratories.

*Limits of the provided data.* The prototyping dataset alone cannot demonstrate the first workflow. Its property block contains one element, no coordinates, an undefined node-to-target mapping and a target that repeats every 8 entries. A model that "succeeds" on it only exploits the ordering, and I reported this rather than a spurious fit. The simulated Track B therefore serves as the canonical property-prediction demonstration.

*Physics-informed elements* (Karniadakis *et al.*, 2021):

- the RBF distance expansion and permutation-invariant pooling build physical symmetries into the GNN;
- the VAE is always evaluated in physical units against a physical-validity window;
- the GP length-scales map directly to physical tolerances (°C, min).

---

## 7. Limitations

- **Simulated data.** The Track B energies come from a documented surrogate potential (Morse + electronegativity term), not DFT. The accuracy reported here measures how well the model learns the structure–property map, not real-material accuracy.
- **Alignment assumption.** Track A uses an assumed descriptor-to-sample alignment.
- **Assumed units and response surface.** The lattice arrays are interpreted as (a, b) in Å. The yield surface (Gaussian, widths 50 °C / 5 min) is assumed; only its optimum, bounds and noise come from the file. BO results depend on that assumed smoothness.
- **Leave-out metric.** The leave-out "min distance over 3 000 samples" metric rewards spread. It should be read together with precision and validity.
- **Software and scale.** Only NumPy/SciPy were available (no PyTorch/scikit-learn, no network access). Models are small and trained on CPU. Hyper-parameters were set a priori and not tuned on test data.
- **Unused modalities.** Microscopy, spectra and text were not present in the provided file, so the multimodal fusion part of the task scope could not be exercised with real data.
